newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, suspending insurer sale, has eye on price.
newsitem.headline: Russia, suspending insurer sale, has eye on price.

text.p: Russia's decision to suspend the sale of its top insurer shows it no longer sees privatisation as a means of creating a reform-friendly private sector, but is now preoccupied primarily with the price, analysts said on Friday.
State Property Committee Chairman Alfred Kokh suspended the privatisation of OAO Rosgosstrakh late on Thursday.
"This testifies to the fact that (First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly) Chubais has changed the main goal of his policy," Moscow Carnegie Endowment senior associate Sergei Markov told Reuters.
"Previously his slogan was privatisation for the sake of reforms, now the slogan is competition for the sake of economic growth."

Chubais spearheaded Russia's privatisation when he became chairman of the newly-formed State Property Committee in 1992. Under his guidance the bulk of the economy was sold within 18 months for vouchers distributed to Russian citizens for free.
President Boris Yeltsin sacked Chubais last year when he became a hate-figure for engineering the speedy and often controversial sales.

Markov said that in the early 1990s the government's main goal was to create a layer of new owners who would support economic reforms. That is why it allowed business groups close to the government to buy company stakes cheaply, he said.

But now that new owners are in place, Chubais, reinstated to the cabinet earlier this year, is politically strong. With new presidential elections planned in three years, economic growth has become his main goal, Markov added.

Under the Rosgosstrakh privatisation scheme, employees bought 20 percent of shares. A nine-member management team has a priority right to buy a further 30 percent at 10.52 roubles per share with a face value of two roubles. The remaining 50 percent was to be sold at an auction at 500 roubles.
Kokh's spokeswoman Viktoriya Vergelskaya said Kokh had suspended the Rosgosstrakh privatisation under the pressure from opponents to the plan.

The State Duma lower house of parliament said Rosgosstrakh was being sold too cheaply, and asked an independent Audit Chamber to look into Rosgosstrakh's privatisation scheme. The chamber found massive violations of law in the plan.
But Vergelskaya said Kokh considered Rosgosstrakh privatisation project legally correct, while the Justice Ministry and the Federation Council upper house of parliament supported his point of view.

Carnegie's Markov said objections to the privatisation were probably based on the low price at which the management team was allowed to snap up its 30 percent, and the size of the stake which would give it huge influence over the running of the firm.

"A small group of managers arranged everything in the way, maybe a legal one, that squeezed out other possible groups from participating in privatisation, which could push the price higher," Markov said.

Rosgosstrakh, together with such giants as telecoms holding company Svyazinvest, oil firm Rosneft and national power company Unified Energy System EESR.RTS, was slated for sale to help the cash-strapped government raise 10 trillion roubles ($1.74 billion) in 1997.
Not one of the sales has gone through yet, possibly signifying a shift from a fire-sale mentality to a more commercially realistic one.
"Now we do not need to be in a hurry with privatisation," said Pavel Kuznetsov, an analyst with the governmental Centre for Economic Reform.
"We have to treat the subject very cautiously, but not stop it. The main goal now is to sell companies as expensively as possible, not as quickly as possible."
The government hopes that a series of sell-offs, together with tax reform and spending cuts, will help the Russian economy start to grow starting next year.
The government forecasts the economy will grow two percent next year and five percent in the year 2000.
But Markov said the Rosgosstrakh decision did not mean the government was bending under pressure from the parliament.
"The attempt to reshuffle the way of privatisation testifies to the changes in Chubais' economic approach," he said.
